facts.claim: The book's central industry is disk drives. 14-inch drives served mainframe makers (200MB+); 8-inch drives, introduced by entrant firms around 1978-1980, served minicomputer makers (10-50MB); 5.25-inch drives (Seagate, 1980) went to desktop PCs after minicomputer makers showed no interest.

The 14-inch makers 'were listening and responding to their established customers'; those customers pulled them along a capacity trajectory of about 22 percent per year. Christensen says the leaders were 'held captive by customers'.
Established firms led nearly every sustaining innovation; their failures were not due to passivity or risk aversion.

Disruptive products offered less of what mainstream customers wanted, and a different set of attributes valued in an emerging market. They were technologically straightforward, often off-the-shelf components in simpler architectures.
Two-thirds of 14-inch makers never entered the 8-inch market; those that did were about two years behind the startups. Every 14-inch maker eventually failed.
The 1.8-inch drive's largest initial market was portable heart monitoring devices, not computing.

Seagate built a working 3.5-inch prototype (around 1985). Its marketing and executive side argued that the market wanted higher-capacity drives at lower cost per megabyte. Prototypes shown to existing customers drew lukewarm reviews; the program manager lowered his sales estimates and executives cancelled the program.

The 3.5-inch architecture was first developed in 1984 by Rodime; Conner Peripherals (a spin-off of Seagate and Miniscribe people) began shipping in 1987, targeting portable and laptop computers. Seagate began making 3.5-inch drives in 1988, then sold them to desktop makers, cutting into its own existing sales.
Critics such as Jill Lepore argue Christensen picked case studies that do not fully support his thesis; disk drives are one focus of that critique.
